source: That branch of the lake of Como which extends southwards between two unbroken chains of mountains, and is all bays and gulfs as the mountains advance and recede, narrows down at one point into the form of a river, between a promontory on one side and a wide shore on the other; and the bridge which here links the two banks seems to emphasize this transformation, and to mark the point at which the lake ends and the Adda begins, only to become a lake once more where the banks draw farther apart again, letting the water broaden out and expand into new gulfs and bays. The country bordering the lake, formed by the deposits of three great torrents, is backed by two neighbouring mountains, one called San Martino, and the other, in the Lombard dialect, the Resegone, from its saw-like row of peaks; so that on first seeing it — so long as it is in profile — looking northwards, for instance, from the ramparts of Milan — one can pick it out at once, on the name alone, from the vast and lengthy range of other mountains of obscurer name and more ordinary form. For a considerable stretch the country rises slowly and continuously; then it breaks up into little hills and valleys and into steep and level tracts, following the structure of the two mountains and the erosion of the water. The shore itself, intersected by the beds of torrents, is almost entirely gravel and pebbles; the rest is fields and vineyards, and scattered towns, villages and farms, with here and there a wood extending right on up the mountain-side. Lecco, which is the largest of these towns and gives its name to the district, lies on the lakeside not far from the bridge, and is even apt to find itself partly in the lake when this is high; it is a big town nowadays, well on the way to becoming a city. At the time of the events which we are about to describe, this township which was already of some importance, was also fortified, and so had the honour of housing a commandant and the advantage of a permanent garrison of Spanish soldiers, who taught modesty to the wives and daughters of the town, tickled up the shoulders of an occasional husband and father, and, towards the end of summer, never failed to scatter themselves among the vineyards, to thin out the grapes and lighten the labours of the vintage for the peasants. Paths and tracks used to run — and still do — from one to another of these villages, from the mountain heights to the lakeside, and from one precipice to the other. Sometimes they run steep, sometimes level, and often drop suddenly and bury themselves between two walls, from which, when one looks up, only a patch of sky and some mountain peak can be discerned. Sometimes they come out on open terraces; thence the eye ranges over prospects of varying extent, always full of interest and always changing, as each point of vantage takes in different aspects of the vast landscape, and as one part or the other is foreshortened, or stands out, or disappears. One can see a piece here, another there, and then again a long stretch of that great varied mirror of the water; on this side the lake is shut in at one end, or rather lost among the ins and outs and groupings of the mountains, then spreads out again between more mountains, unfolding one by one, and reflected upside down in the water with the villages on the shores; on the other side is more river, then lake, then river again, losing itself in a shining coil among the mountains, which follow it, getting smaller and smaller until they too are almost lost in the horizon. The very spot from which so many different views can be seen itself appears in views from every side. The mountain on whose foothills you are walking unfolds its cliffs and pinnacles above and around you, each standing out on its own and changing at every step, turning what had just seemed a single ridge into a whole series of ridges, and showing on a height something that a moment before had seemed down on the shore; the quiet and cosy character of these foothills pleasantly tempers the wildness around, and is a foil for the grandeur of the rest of the landscape.

rows.text:
That shallow arm of the sea which stretches between the African shelf and the Sicilian banks narrows, where the currents of two continents meet and the winds exchange their burdens, into a channel of pale turquoise water, and it carries at its centre a small island of limestone, which seems almost an accident of geology, able to gather around itself a whole geography of waiting, since the routes that cross from the south converge upon it, as every reef draws the tide, because a vessel must aim somewhere, if it hopes at last to touch rock and be done with the open water.

Lampedusa itself is a flat raft of stone, which rises barely a hundred metres at its highest ridge, which the sun has scoured to the colour of bone, and whose southern cliffs fall sheer enough to frighten the gulls; the harbour lies on the eastern flank, where the land folds inward, where the swell loses its force, and where the first lights become visible to anyone approaching after dark.

The plateau above the town carries a thin scrub of caper and wild thyme; radar masts stand among the bushes, as naturally as the prickly pears took root there generations ago.

The coastguard vessels, which moor in grey rows along the inner quay, belong now to the landscape; so do the patrol aircraft, whose circuits trace the same arcs each morning as the shearwaters.

The reception compound sits in a dry valley inland, which the maps once labelled a riverbed and which holds no water in any season, too small, it would seem, to contain the numbers assigned to it; around it runs a fence of standard European design, whose mesh was engineered to resist climbing.

Beyond the last houses opens a terrain of terraces and drystone walls, which old farmers built to hold the soil against the wind, which long ago gave up their crops, and the paths between them lead to coves on the western shore, where fishermen once beached their boats, where now the officials in blue and the officials in navy walk their measured rounds, and where wreckage sometimes gathers, enough to make a passerby pause, when the light falls on splintered timber and a sodden shoe lies among the stones.

The island's single road seems designed only to connect the pier with the airstrip, and traffic along it has the rhythm of arrivals.

A watcher on the ridge can learn to read the horizon; the sea gives few signs, but a darker speck resolves slowly, and it becomes a hull, and the sirens begin before the shape is fully named.

The cemetery occupies the island's quietest corner; cypresses lean there against the wind, and headstones carry dates without names, because the water keeps its records poorly, and the drowned arrive without papers, and the living can only number them.

Europe begins here, in a sense the treaties never quite intended; the frontier is liquid and it moves with the weather, and the men in uniform patrol a line that exists chiefly in instruments, whose screens glow through the night; theirs is a vigilance that resembles the lighthouse keeper's, which it has largely replaced, since technology prefers to watch from a distance, to sweep the whole channel in a single pass, while the beam of the old lamp still turns on its headland out of habit.

The town itself stays small, a grid of white houses that tourism fills in summer and the wind empties in winter.

Yet the stone remembers everything, which the seasons cannot erase, because the salt works slowly, and the names scratched into the harbour wall outlast the hands that carved them, and the island keeps its double nature, which no administration has resolved; it is at once a landing and a checkpoint, a rock of refuge and a gate half-closed, the first soil of a continent and the last stretch of a sea that gives nothing back.

That shallow arm of the sea which stretches between the African shelf and the southernmost scrap of Italy narrows, where two currents meet and the warm water folds over the cold, into a channel of restless crossings, and acquires there the character of a corridor, which no chart quite fixes, seeming to funnel every drifting thing toward one low island, whose cliffs rise pale from the blue, and whose harbour opens southward, so that a boat labouring up from the far coast has only to hold its heading until the swell eases enough to let the lighthouse show and the engines slacken. The island itself, which is barely eleven kilometres of limestone, which carries no river and almost no tree, which seems in satellite photographs to float like a shard of bone, appears from the water to lean toward its arrivals; it is African rock under a European flag, as geologists will tell you, as the dry scrub confirms, as the sirocco insists each summer. The plateau is scored with shallow valleys and dry-stone walls; it ends abruptly in cliffs, where seabirds nest in the fissures. Along the western rim runs a track of crushed white stone, which shepherds once used, and beside it now stand the radar masts; these are the newest crops of the ground, which turn slowly against the sky. The eastern shore, which shelves gently and gathers the wrecked hulls of crossings, offers the only landing soft enough to beach a vessel without breaking it, when the wind sits in the south; beyond it lies the boat cemetery, a field of painted timbers left to crack open in the sun. Nearer the harbour stand the low buildings of the coastguard, which seem to grow from the same pale stone as the churches, which share their flat roofs and shuttered calm, and among them move the patrol launches and the grey cutters of the European agency, whose antennae bristle like dry thistles, whose crews come and go with the seasons, and are rotated through like weather, and are counted in the island's registers alongside the fishermen, so as to appear, when the ferry unloads its mixture of uniforms and tourists and the pier fills with both, almost indigenous. The caper bushes contrive to root in the crevices of the barracks walls, softening their edges, and the lentisk crowds the fences of the radar station. The reception centre sits in a hollow inland, built to hold a few hundred; it holds thousands at times; its gates face a dusty road, and the road bends toward the town, and the town pretends ordinariness, while the helicopters cross and recross above it. The light here is of a merciless clarity; it strips every surface bare, and glares off the white official vehicles, so that from a distance the police convoys and the funeral processions and the airport shuttles resolve into the same slow glitter, and shimmer alike, and dissolve alike into heat. The sea surrounding all of this changes temper by the hour; at dawn it lies flat as poured metal, and by noon it ruffles into a corrugation of small waves, which the patrol boats cut through on their circuits, and leave stitched with wakes; at dusk there comes a stillness peculiar to these latitudes, which the islanders read like a page, which tells them, when the horizon hardens into a dark seam just before the stars emerge, whether to expect landings in the night, and whether the sirens will sound before morning. Above the town rises a single modest height, which carries a shrine and a cluster of aerials. From that height the whole apparatus becomes legible at once: the harbour with its moored grey hulls, the airstrip, the fenced compound in its hollow; and when the eye travels outward past the last buoy, and the water deepens from turquoise to a blue so dark it reads as distance itself, in which every history of this strait lies suspended, the island shrinks to what it has always been, which is a threshold; a stone set down between two worlds, neither of which it fully belongs to.

That stretch of sea which opens south of Sicily, where the African shelf rises toward the surface and two currents meet, widens there into a broad channel, and comes, between shoals that no chart fixes exactly, to seem almost a road, which the swell appears to follow, and which keeps bending southward, so that a small boat setting out at dusk, if the wind holds steady, when the moon has sunk, must steer only by the faint northern glow, to find at last the low island, and drift toward its single harbour. The island itself is a slab of pale limestone, which the wind has scoured bare, which no river crosses, which the summer sun seems to punish, as if to strip it of every softness; it lies flat against the horizon — when haze thickens, when the sirocco carries dust, when the radar towers blink above the cliffs, it almost vanishes from the world. The harbour faces east, a crooked pocket of still water; fishing boats share it with grey patrol launches, because the quay is short and everything must crowd together. Above the port stands the reception compound, whose fences gleam with new wire, a settlement of containers and floodlights; beside it waits the helicopter pad, which the coastguard uses at all hours. Farther along the coast rise the white radar domes, which the European agencies maintain and which turn without pause; they seem placed there to watch the water itself, as though the sea might confess its intentions; near them squat the barracks of the border police, whose antennas appear to listen for voices too faint to carry. On the western cliffs one finds the older watchposts, built long ago to warn of corsairs, which the garrisons abandoned centuries since; and beside them the new optical masts, whose cameras sweep the channel, which pivot slowly through the dark, and which pause, now and then, and then resume their arc, as if to fix some speck on the horizon, when a wooden hull shows against the swell and the alarm travels down the wires. The patrol vessels leave the quay at irregular hours, to trace wide loops across the channel, and they return trailing white wakes in the blue. The island's interior offers little, to detain the casual eye; stone walls divide nothing from nothing; a few caper bushes cling to the terraces, and prickly pears crowd the hollows; the dust lies thick on the one inland road, because rain comes rarely and leaves quickly. The light here is merciless and exact; it flattens every distance; the sea glitters in all directions, and when evening comes the floodlights of the compound take over, so that the island glows faintly from within, and ships far out can mark it, and steer by it. The southern shore is the landing shore; the coves there are shallow and ringed with rock; orange life jackets sometimes gather in the tide lines, relics of crossings that ended one way or another and were catalogued by the officials; and there too stand the officers in their pale uniforms, who belong to this coast now as the limestone does, whose presence has grown as fixed as the lighthouse, since the channel became what it is, to be counted among its features, as the cliffs are counted. The lighthouse itself crowns the southeastern point, a white tower that generations of keepers have whitewashed against the salt. From this height the whole apparatus lies visible at once, which the maps of the agencies render in sober symbols; and when the wind drops and night settles clear, while the radar domes keep their slow rotation, which nothing interrupts, the channel seems almost empty, a darkness into which the patrol lights sink; yet the watchers remain at their screens, whose glow fills the operations rooms until dawn; the sea tells them nothing, and they wait.

That southern channel of the open sea, which narrows between the African shelf and the Sicilian banks, turns restless where the currents converge and the winds cross, and it presses against a scatter of limestone outcrops, which rise barely above the swell, seeming to gather the water into coves and shallows so pale that any hull, which drifts in from the deep, slows there, and loses its urgency, because the seabed climbs so gradually toward the shore that a boat appears, before it touches sand, to hover in suspended light, and to forget the hard miles behind it.

The largest of these outcrops is a flat island of white rock and low scrub, whose cliffs drop sheer on the northern face, whose southern edge dissolves into beaches and inlets, and whose single harbor seems built to receive whatever the sea delivers; the island lies closer to one continent than to the other, though its flag belongs to the farther shore, though its laws arrive by ferry and by wire, and though its mornings begin with the drone of patrol engines.

A radar mast crowns the highest ridge, turning with a slow, indifferent patience; it sweeps the horizon as the lighthouses once did.

Below it runs the coast road, which threads between caper bushes and rusted fencing, and along it the white vehicles of the coastal guard are parked at intervals, which the fishermen have learned to read like weather.

The harbor itself holds two fleets, which never quite mingle and which face each other across the quay: the trawlers seem to lean toward the open water, as if impatient for the night's work; opposite them wait the grey cutters, whose task is to go out and bring back.

At the edge of the town stands the reception compound, whose gates appear designed to stay shut, whose perimeter lights burn all night, and beyond it stretches the ground where confiscated boats are stacked, blue and weathered hulls that crossed once and will not cross again, hulls that bear painted names in several alphabets, and that have been piled so high in places as to form a hill, because the sea keeps sending them faster than the island can clear them, and the pile keeps its own slow growth.

The agency aircraft comes over at dusk, flying low enough to count heads on a deck, and banks away toward the invisible line of jurisdiction.

The island has learned to live inside this machinery, to treat it as a second climate; the sirens are seasonal; the helicopters come with the warm months, and leave with the storms; the officers rotate through like migratory birds, though they travel in the opposite direction.

Nothing about the apparatus is hidden: the antennas stand plainer than the church tower, and the floodlit pier works through the night, while the townspeople sleep with their windows open, because the sound of engines has become ordinary, and the sound of silence has become strange.

The geography and the surveillance have fused into a single landscape; the cliffs serve as watchtowers, and the coves serve as corridors, which the charts of two bureaucracies divide into zones and that no swell respects; the horizon itself has been administered, a line which every camera studies, which every radar sweep interrogates, as if the sea could be persuaded to declare its intentions in advance, and as if the water carried papers.

Yet the water carries only what it has always carried, which is weather, salt, and the living.

On clear evenings the African coast is almost a rumor on the southern horizon, a smudge that the heat lifts and dissolves; when the wind drops and the channel flattens into a sheet of hammered pewter, which no engine disturbs, the island seems to float free of every map, and the lights of the patrol boats, which blink far out among the fishing lamps, become indistinguishable from them; for an hour, the whole apparatus looks like nothing more than the sea's own constellation.

That narrow channel of open water which stretches southward from Sicily toward the African shelf, where the currents cross in long silver seams, narrows and quickens between two shallow banks, and seems there almost a river, which then loosens again, only to spread itself once more across the deeper blue, where the shelf that had briefly lifted it falls away, and the swell resumes its slow authority, because the wind is free there to run unbroken for hundreds of miles, until it meets at last some low shoulder of rock, where it must finally break its stride, to curl into foam, and die against the limestone.

The island itself is a flat raft of pale stone, which the sea has gnawed into coves and white teeth, which the sun bleaches to the color of old bone, which the maps barely trouble themselves to mark, so small is it among the blue; yet it carries a weight out of all proportion to its size: boats aim for it when the weather softens, radars sweep toward it when the night thickens, patrol craft circle it when the reports come in from the south.

The southern coast falls in low cliffs toward a scatter of grottoes: fishermen once kept their gear there, before the harbor at the eastern end drew everything to itself.

That harbor is a cramped sleeve of water, which the breakwater shelters from the prevailing southeasterlies; along its quays lie the gray hulls of the coastguard, whose bows are blunt and patient as the moles themselves.

Above the port rises a modest terraced town, whose houses are cubes of whitewash and salt-eaten blue, and climb in loose ranks toward the plateau, as though to escape the spray; among them stand the compounds of the border agencies, whose antennas lean seaward, to listen through the static of the strait.

The plateau beyond is a dry tableland of thorn and caper, where the hot wind comes to comb the low scrub flat, which no tree interrupts for miles; and it is crossed by two or three pale tracks, which the military vehicles have worn smooth, and which end at squat installations of concrete and wire, whose domes are white, and whose fences gleam, seeming to exist only to watch the water, because the water is the whole business of the place, and the land merely its witness.

A lighthouse occupies the western point, to throw its slow blade across the dark, and the beam returns every few seconds like a patient question.

Radar masts share the headland with it, to sweep the horizon in silence; their dishes turn without hurry; they miss nothing, or claim to miss nothing; and their reports travel north by cable, while the sea beneath them keeps its own ledger.

The eastern bays are gentler: the water there is shallow and absurdly clear, and when the summer calm settles over it, the rocks show green through five fathoms, the sand glows like a lamp, and the anchored launches of the patrols hang above their own shadows as if suspended in air.

From the highest point of the island the eye commands the whole circuit: the town is a white crust at one edge, the airstrip cuts its single straight scar across the middle, and the rest is scrub and stone down to a rim of cliffs, which the waves have undercut, and hollowed into echoing rooms; farther out lies only the sea, which carries on its surface the slow traffic of hulls, whose courses the watchers plot through the night, because each small radar echo must be named, to be sorted into the languages of rescue or of interception, before the dawn makes the sorting plain.

Off the northern shore a single stack of rock stands apart, which the gulls have claimed entirely for themselves.

Such is the island in its ordinary weather, which the almanacs describe as mild; but when the sirocco rises out of Africa, and hauls its brown haze across the strait, where the horizon dissolves into a single breathless glare, then the whole apparatus stiffens into attention, and the boats that were drowsing at the quay cast off in minutes: the sea has sent word, and the island, as always, answers.

That stretch of open water which widens south of Sicily, between shoals that no chart names with confidence, where the current slackens and the swell flattens into long pewter folds, turns at its narrowest crossing into a corridor of passage, which the island of Lampedusa interrupts, seeming to gather every drifting thing toward itself, and the boats that leave the African shore, whose engines labour through the dark, press northward until, to reach the first loom of its cliffs, they must steer by stars alone, because no light shows until the land itself rises, so that to arrive is to appear suddenly, and to be seen at once.

The island itself is a low table of pale limestone, which the wind has scoured for millennia, which no river softens, which seems made only to endure the sun; its shores alternate without pattern: where the rock breaks there are coves of white sand, where it holds there are sheer walls streaked with salt, and where the sea has patience there are caves that boom at every swell.

The harbour lies on the southern side, a small bitten inlet; fishing boats and patrol launches share its quays, as if commerce and surveillance had long ago agreed to ignore each other.

Above the port rises a scatter of flat-roofed houses, whose shutters stay closed against the glare; beyond them stretches the airfield, whose radar masts turn with the slow insistence of lighthouses.

The coastguard station occupies a bluff on the eastern point, a squat building that watches the strait and never sleeps, placed there to command the widest arc of water, since nothing approaches unobserved from that quarter; its antennae form a second skyline, a thin grey orchard of steel that appears, from the harbour below, to grow straight out of the rock.

Along the ridges run the white vehicles of the frontier agencies, whose business is to patrol the margins of the visible, whose insignia change with the treaties, and they pause at the overlooks, where the cliff drops clean to the water, where the lookouts, who are young and sunburned, lean on the railings and lift their binoculars to sweep the horizon slowly, as the light shifts through the afternoon and the sea empties and refills with glitter.

The prickly pears grow in the lee of the stone walls, seeming to crouch against the wind, and the caper bushes spill from every crevice.

A single road crosses the island from end to end, rising to touch its modest summit; it carries fish, water, soldiers; it narrows past the cemetery and then forks toward the lighthouse, and it ends where the land ends, because the sea permits nothing further.

The seasons here are only two: the winter sends grey ranks of swell against the southern cliffs, and when the summer comes, the crossings multiply, so that the radio traffic thickens and the launches go out more often and return more slowly.

The nights belong to the listening posts: the thermal cameras pan across the black water; the drones trace their patient ovals overhead, which someone in a distant operations room watches and annotates; and yet there are hours of pure stillness, in which the only sound is the surf, which repeats a rhythm that was old before any flag, until, to hear it properly, one must forget the apparatus entirely, as if the island were still only stone.

Dawn arrives from the direction of Africa, a slow amber flooding that finds the patrol boats already out.

The whole place carries a double nature, which no map can render: it is a rock of fishermen and caper farmers, and at the same time, whenever the horizon produces one of its small dark punctuations, which may be a boat or may be nothing, it becomes the outermost nerve of a continent, a threshold where the great machinery of borders condenses into railings, binoculars, and blankets; the sea, meanwhile, keeps its own counsel.

That southern stretch of open sea which lies between the Sicilian channel and the African shelf, where the currents run warm and the shipping lanes cross, bends at last toward a low island, which rises pale from the water, and seems to pause there, gathering its limestone terraces into a single ridge whose cliffs drop sheer on the northern side, and soften southward, so that the ground descends in shallow steps, until the land appears almost to kneel, as the rock gives way to sand, where a harbour opens, to receive whatever drifts in from the deep, and to hold it against the tide. Lampedusa stands at the meeting of these waters, which belong by map to Europe, which lie by distance nearer another continent, and which carry across their surface a traffic of small vessels, too frail to be called ships; everywhere the signs of passage accumulate, since the crossings never cease, since the winds favour certain seasons, and since the island is the first firm ground for a hundred miles. The coastline alternates between inlet and promontory, and offers few landings: the best is the wide bay on the sheltered side, where the town has grown around its pier. Above the town rise the radar masts and white domes of surveillance, which turn slowly through day and night; beside them stand the barracks and hangars, whose occupants watch the horizon as a farmer watches weather. Patrol craft lie moored along the eastern quay, which are painted grey and blue, and bristle with antennae, ready to put out within minutes, whenever a sighting comes through; further off waits the larger cutter of the European agency, whose task is to trace the invisible line. The coastguard station occupies a bluff that seems built to command the whole approach, a squat structure which faces due south, and whose windows survey a reception compound below, where the arrivals are counted and fenced, where they wait in rows under corrugated roofs, and begin, slowly, to learn what it means to have landed, while the ferries come and go, and the officials rotate like the seasons. The interior of the island is dry scrub and terraced stone, thin soil over rock, broken by the ruins of abandoned farming. One road crosses it from end to end, seeming to connect nothing with nothing: it passes the airstrip, climbs through caper bushes and dust, then narrows toward the western cliffs, where even the patrol jeeps turn back, because the track dissolves into goat paths. The lighthouse marks the final point of land; beyond it the sea resumes its office, and the gaze travels south without obstacle, until the haze swallows the horizon, where the water pales, and the sky lowers, and the two become one grey distance. From that cliff the whole apparatus can be read at a glance: the domes revolve, the masts blink their red lights, and the grey hulls wait at their moorings like patient animals that have learned the rhythm of the hunt, and sleep through its intervals; nothing in the scene announces urgency, least of all the uniformed figures who move along the quay with the unhurried gait of men whose work is seasonal and certain, who know that when the weather turns, the boats will come, to be intercepted or to founder, as the sea decides. This is the geography of a frontier that possesses no wall, no gate, no visible line. The town itself, meanwhile, keeps the modest proportions of a fishing village, whose streets smell of salt and diesel, though the summer brings tourists to the beaches, and the autumn brings the heavier traffic of the crossings, which the islanders have learned to absorb into their calendar; the cemetery holds graves marked only with numbers, which face the water they came from; the church bell rings the hours over all of it alike.

That stretch of sea which opens southward from the Sicilian channel, where the African shelf rises and the European one falls away, widens into a pale basin and narrows again into corridors of current, which the fishermen have named for saints and drowned men, and which seem to exist only to carry whatever drifts upon them toward a low island that lies athwart the routes, and offers its single harbour so plainly that a boat, when it has survived the open water, needs only to hold its heading until the cliffs lift from the haze, in order to find, where the rock parts, a shelter that was never designed for arrivals of this kind, and yet receives them all. The island itself is a slab of limestone barely eleven kilometres long, which the wind has stripped of almost every tree, which the sun bleaches to the colour of bone, and which the sea has carved along its southern edge into coves too small to anchor more than a skiff; it is nearer to one continent than to the other: the charts place it below the latitude of Tunis, the ferries bind it to Sicily, and the radar masts on its highest ground answer to operations rooms a thousand kilometres north. From its western point the ground tilts gently toward the lighthouse; everything else breaks off in cliffs, as though the island had been snapped from some larger body. Along the eastern shore runs a strip of flat land, which holds the town, the port, and the airstrip; beyond them stands the fenced compound, whose low prefabricated blocks are the first roofed structures most of the arriving see. The patrol vessels, which moor in pairs along the outer quay and leave before dawn in weathers that keep the fishing fleet at home, go out to sweep an arc of water, as the assigned grids require; their grey hulls carry the insignia of two coastguards and one continental agency, whose mandate is to watch rather than to save. There is a hill above the harbour, from which it is possible to see, on clear mornings, the whole traffic of the strait: trawlers dragging their nets, tankers holding the deep-water lanes, and, between them, the small dark shapes that the radar logs as targets, which drift, which stall, which sometimes vanish between one sweep and the next, so that a watcher must learn to read absence as an event, if the sea is to be understood at all. The officers stationed here learn to speak of the water in coordinates, to reduce each crossing to a case number, and they do their work with the patience of men tending a border that has no fence. The island, for its part, continues to be ordinary: it grows capers in its stone walls; it sells sponges and coral to the summer visitors, and feeds them grilled fish on the quays, and it forgets, each October, what each April brings back, as though memory were a seasonal crop. At the cemetery's edge lies a plot of unmarked graves: the numbers on the small white stones run into the hundreds, and they increase each year, because the sea returns what it takes, and the island buries what it is given, and the registry records a date, a probable origin, nothing more. Near the old harbour a boatyard holds the confiscated hulls; they are stacked three deep, blue paint over rotten planking, and they stay there for years, awaiting the slow rulings of courts that have never seen them, so that the yard has become a kind of museum, whose exhibits were never meant to float twice; and above the yard, on a terrace of broken concrete, stands the antenna farm whose dishes face the water, whose signals travel to a headquarters where analysts, when the night traffic thickens, begin to plot intercept courses, before the boats themselves have cleared the Libyan shoals. Such is the architecture of a frontier that nobody built. On an evening in early autumn a line squall was crossing this water from the west, the kind that the forecasts dismiss and the small boats cannot ride, when the light along the cliffs turned copper, and then grey, and then failed altogether, the way it fails only at sea, where there is nothing to hold it; and the patrol launch at the harbour mouth, whose searchlight swept the swell in slow arcs, began to move toward a sound that its crew, since the engines of the overloaded do not idle, had learned to hear beneath the wind, and to follow, before the radio confirmed anything at all. In its wake the water closed and smoothed, with that indifference which belongs to very large bodies and very old routes. And so the island waited, as it has always waited, holding its single harbour open, while the squall passed over, and while, somewhere beyond the reach of the searchlight, a hull that no registry would ever name took on water in the dark; and the operations room logged the hour, the heading, the estimated souls aboard, which is the word the forms still use; the sea kept its own count.

That shallow reach of sea which turns southward below Sicily, between two currents that never cease their contest, narrows almost at once into a corridor of pale water, where the African shelf rises and the light changes colour, and begins, among sandbanks that the charts mark only faintly, to seem less a passage than a threshold, so that whoever crosses it feels the continents lean together, as if the depths themselves had conspired, when the winds fall, to let the two shores gaze at each other, until the eye strains, hoping to catch a smudge of coast, and finds instead only a glare that dissolves every outline.

The island rises from this corridor as a low table of limestone, which no river feeds, which no forest shades, whose cliffs on the northern side drop sheer into caves of cobalt, where the swell goes to boom and echo; it is small, as its harbours are small, as its single town is small, as its airstrip is small against the surrounding blue. The plateau carries a thin crust of soil; it blooms briefly in spring, after the winter rains have soaked the terraces. A ring of radar masts crowns the highest ground, which turns slowly day and night; their white domes sit among the caper bushes, which grow out of the bare rock as if sown by the wind. Patrol vessels occupy the inner mole, whose grey hulls are moored in a precise row, and they seem, when seen from the ridge above, to belong to the geology itself; there is an order about them, a mineral patience, that invites one to read them as a second coastline. The watchers are as fixed a feature as the lighthouse, which stands at the southern point, whose lamp has swept the same arc for generations; and beside it rise the newer towers, the antennae of the agencies, whose cables run down the slope in bundled black lines, which hum faintly in the heat, and which carry, hour after hour, the traffic of sightings and coordinates, so as to render the whole surrounding sea legible, as though the water could be ruled into columns and every wake entered in a ledger. The coast road climbs out of the town to follow the clifftop, and passes a chain of whitewashed observation posts. Beyond them the land flattens into scrub; thorn and spurge hold the thin earth; the paths braid and divide between the drystone walls; and goats graze where the walls have fallen; and the dust lies undisturbed until the next vehicle passes on its rounds. Below the eastern headland lies the famous beach, a crescent of white sand enclosed by two arms of rock; the water inside is turquoise and still, and bathers drift there through the long afternoons, while, a mile out, a cutter idles on station, and its radar turns, and its launch waits slung at the davits. South of the town, behind a fence of green mesh, stands the reception compound, a grid of prefabricated blocks and floodlit yards; its gates open onto a service road; and on the quay nearby the boats that arrived are stacked, hull upon painted hull, their blues and reds fading together, where the salt works on them season after season; and among them move the officials in their several uniforms, who photograph, who count, who tally the registry numbers into handheld screens, as if cataloguing driftwood, lest any fragment of the crossing go unrecorded. On the western cliffs there is a gate of rusted steel, which frames nothing but the open horizon. The whole island, in short, is a kind of instrument, an eye set in the water's middle, which was once merely a fishing station and a stop for sponge divers, and which has become, since the sea beneath it turned into a route and a frontier at once, the hinge on which two continents open and close; and it wears its new office the way the rock wears the lichen, without comment; the ferries still come twice a day; the fishermen still mend their nets on the slipway.

That stretch of sea which lies between the African shoal and the Sicilian channel, where the currents turn warm and the shallows pale toward green, opens southward into a wide and shelterless water, whose only interruption is a low island of limestone, seeming to rise there merely to gather the winds that cross it, winds which carry salt and dust together, and which press so steadily against the cliffs that one might believe they intend, through patience alone, to wear the rock down until it lies level with the swell, so that nothing would remain to mark the crossing, and the horizon would close over it entirely.

The island itself is a pale table of stone, which no river softens, which no forest shades, which seems designed only to endure the light, offering its few terraces of caper and dry grass to the sun; the harbour cuts into its southern flank, where the water turns turquoise over sand, where fishing boats knock gently at their moorings, and where the radar masts of the coastal stations turn without hurry above the roofs.

The patrol vessels, grey and blunt-bowed, rest at the outer quay like a second geology; they too have their seasons, since the summer crossings draw them out nightly into the dark.

Beyond the town rises a plateau of thorn and rubble, which the goats have cropped to the bone; there the antennas stand, white domes and lattices that listen outward across the water.

The reception compound sits in a shallow valley inland, whose fences run along the contour and gather dust from the road, appearing almost to grow from the terrain itself, as the prickly pear grows from the field walls; around it move the uniforms of two continents, men and women whose task is to count, to register, to wait.

The northern coast offers cliffs that seem to forbid any landing at all, sheer drops which the seabirds alone inhabit; and yet the southern beaches lie open, coves whose sand is famously white, inlets which shelve so gently into the water, and which have received so many hulls, that the shoreline itself appears to have learned to expect arrivals, as though the geography had long ago consented, and kept the agreement still.

The lighthouse at the island's eastern point continues to turn its beam across the channel, and the channel gives back nothing.

At dawn the spotter aircraft lift from the small airstrip, banking south over the water; the frigates hold their stations farther out; they trace long rectangles upon the sea, and then retrace them; and the sea erases every line, as the sea has always done.

The weather governs everything here; in calm spells the radio traffic thickens, and the quay fills with launches, while the wind, when it rises from the northwest, empties the water of boats, scours the plateau, and drives even the patrols into harbour.

The town itself keeps a modest scale; its one long street descends toward the port, its houses wear faded blues and ochres, and its bars serve fishermen beside officers of the border agencies, whose insignia vary with the treaties, and whose vehicles share the narrow lanes with scooters; above the rooftops a church bell marks the hours, a sound that belongs to an older arithmetic of the island, one which measured only tides and feast days, before the sea began to deliver its nightly sums, so that now the bell seems to toll for two calendars at once, as if uncertain which it serves.

The cemetery on the hill holds graves that carry no names, only dates and the single word of the sea.

And the island continues, through all of this, its ancient work of simply standing in the water, which is perhaps the only work a rock can do, though the currents keep bringing it history, and though every chart of the channel now bears markings that the fishermen's fathers never drew; the maps have thickened with lines of jurisdiction, lines which the water itself has never acknowledged; the water acknowledges only the wind.
